Thera Bank — Credit Card Customer Churn Prediction (Refreshed)¶

Objective: Identify customers likely to attrite (close their credit card account) so Thera Bank can act on retention before they leave, and quantify which behavioral/demographic factors drive that risk.

This version extends the original analysis with: corrected missing-value handling, class-specific (not accuracy/weighted) metrics, XGBoost/LightGBM/stacked-ensemble comparison, SHAP explainability, and a cost-sensitive threshold analysis tying the model to rupee impact.

Data Quality Check¶

The original submission of this analysis stated there were no missing values in this dataset. That was incorrect — checking explicitly below.

In [5]:
missing = df.isnull().sum()
missing = missing[missing > 0]
print("Columns with missing values:\n", missing)
print("\nIncome_Category unique values:", df['Income_Category'].unique())

Columns with missing values:
 Education_Level    1519
Marital_Status      749
dtype: int64

Income_Category unique values: <StringArray>
[   '$60K - $80K', 'Less than $40K',   '$80K - $120K',    '$40K - $60K',
        '$120K +',            'abc']
Length: 6, dtype: str

Findings:

  • Education_Level has 1,519 missing values (~15%) and Marital_Status has 749 (~7.4%) — genuine NaNs, not the "no missing values" originally reported.
  • Income_Category contains 1,112 rows with the garbage value "abc" instead of a real income bracket — a data-entry/export error, not a NaN, but it needs the same treatment.

Rationale for treatment: Checked below whether missingness itself correlates with churn (i.e., whether customers who don't disclose education/marital status behave differently). The difference is small (~1 percentage point), so there's no strong signal to engineer a "missingness" flag feature. Instead of imputing a fake mode value (which would misrepresent real customers), all three issues are mapped to an explicit "Unknown" category — for categorical fields, "unknown" is itself informative and preserves customers who declined to share the field, without inventing data that wasn't collected.

2. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

2.1 Problem Definition — class balance¶

Churn is the core problem: how imbalanced is it, and what does that imply for modeling and metric choice downstream?

In [8]:
churn_counts = df['Attrition_Flag'].value_counts()
churn_pct = df['Attrition_Flag'].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
axes[0].pie(churn_counts, labels=churn_counts.index, autopct='%1.1f%%',
            colors=['#4C72B0', '#DD8452'], startangle=90)
axes[0].set_title('Customer Attrition Split')

sns.countplot(data=df, x='Attrition_Flag', ax=axes[1], palette=['#4C72B0', '#DD8452'])
axes[1].set_title('Customer Attrition Counts')
for i, v in enumerate(churn_counts):
    axes[1].text(i, v + 50, str(v), ha='center')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Attrited customers: {churn_counts['Attrited Customer']} ({churn_pct['Attrited Customer']:.1f}%)")
print(f"Existing customers: {churn_counts['Existing Customer']} ({churn_pct['Existing Customer']:.1f}%)")

Attrited customers: 1627 (16.1%)
Existing customers: 8500 (83.9%)

Observation: churn is ~16% of the base — a meaningfully imbalanced problem. This has two direct consequences carried through the rest of the notebook: (1) plain accuracy is a misleading metric, since predicting "no churn" for everyone already scores ~84%; (2) class-imbalance handling (SMOTE/undersampling) and class-specific recall/precision/F1 are the right lens, not overall accuracy.

Key bivariate observations (with numbers):

  • Attrited customers transact far less: median Total_Trans_Ct and the medians printed above make the gap explicit rather than just visual — this is the single strongest visual separator in the boxplots.
  • Total_Revolving_Bal is dramatically lower for attrited customers — consistent with churners winding down card usage before formally closing the account.
  • Months_Inactive_12_mon is higher for attrited customers — inactivity precedes attrition, which is actionable (a re-engagement trigger after 2-3 inactive months).
  • Total_Ct_Chng_Q4_Q1 (transaction count momentum) is lower for churners — a declining trend into Q1 is a leading indicator, not just a low absolute level.

Multicollinearity flag: Credit_Limit and Avg_Open_To_Buy are correlated at ~0.996 — expected, since Avg_Open_To_Buy ≈ Credit_Limit − Total_Revolving_Bal, so one is almost entirely redundant given the other two. This is addressed explicitly in preprocessing below (dropping Avg_Open_To_Buy) rather than left in silently.

The pairplot shows Total_Trans_Ct vs Total_Trans_Amt separating attrited (orange) from existing (blue) customers reasonably cleanly in the lower-left region — low count and low amount together is a stronger churn signal than either alone, which is exactly the kind of interaction a tree-based model can exploit but a single univariate cutoff can't.

EDA takeaways carried into modeling:

  1. Churn is ~16% of customers — imbalance must be explicitly handled and evaluated with class-specific metrics.
  2. Engagement/activity features (Total_Trans_Ct, Total_Trans_Amt, Total_Revolving_Bal, Months_Inactive_12_mon) show the clearest separation by churn status and are the likely top drivers — checked formally against SHAP later.
  3. Credit_Limit and Avg_Open_To_Buy are collinear (r≈0.996) — drop one before modeling.
  4. Card_Category is heavily imbalanced within itself — interpret per-category churn-rate differences cautiously given small sample sizes in Gold/Platinum/Silver.
  5. Missingness in Education_Level/Marital_Status does not itself predict churn — safe to treat as a plain "Unknown" category rather than engineering a missingness flag.

3. Data Preprocessing¶

Steps: missing-value treatment (already applied above with rationale), outlier check, multicollinearity fix, encoding, and train/test split — with no leakage (all transformations fit on train only where applicable).

3.1 Outlier detection¶

In [17]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 6))
sns.boxplot(data=df[num_features], ax=ax)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
ax.set_title('Outlier scan — numerical features (raw scale)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for col in ['Credit_Limit', 'Total_Trans_Amt']:
    q99 = df[col].quantile(0.99)
    pct_above = (df[col] > q99).mean() * 100
    print(f"{col}: 99th pct = {q99:.0f}, {pct_above:.2f}% of rows above it")

Credit_Limit: 99th pct = 34516, 0.00% of rows above it
Total_Trans_Amt: 99th pct = 15882, 1.01% of rows above it

Rationale: Credit_Limit and Total_Trans_Amt show long right tails (high-limit/high-spend customers), but every model used downstream — Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, Bagging, XGBoost, LightGBM — is tree-based and splits on rank/threshold, not raw magnitude, so extreme values do not distort the fit the way they would for a linear or distance-based model. Outliers are therefore not capped or removed: doing so would risk deleting exactly the high-value, high-limit customers who are business-critical to retain, without any modeling benefit given the model family in use. This decision is stated explicitly rather than defaulted into.

4. Model Building — Original (Imbalanced) Data¶

Metric choice: given the ~84/16 imbalance, accuracy and average='weighted' metrics are misleading — a model predicting "no churn" for everyone scores ~84% accuracy while catching zero churners. All metrics below are reported for the churn (positive) class specifically, which is the class that actually matters for the business problem.

Models compared: Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, Bagging (the original five), plus XGBoost and LightGBM added for this refresh.

In [21]:
def evaluate(name, model, X_tr, y_tr, X_te, y_te, results_dict):
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    pred = model.predict(X_te)
    proba = model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    row = {
        'Recall (churn)': recall_score(y_te, pred),
        'Precision (churn)': precision_score(y_te, pred),
        'F1 (churn)': f1_score(y_te, pred),
        'Accuracy': accuracy_score(y_te, pred),
        'ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_te, proba),
    }
    results_dict[name] = row
    return model

base_models = {
    'Decision Tree': DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    'Random Forest': RandomForestClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    'Gradient Boosting': GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    'AdaBoost': AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    'Bagging': BaggingClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    'XGBoost': XGBClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, eval_metric='logloss'),
    'LightGBM': LGBMClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, verbose=-1),
}

results_original = {}
fitted_original = {}
for name, m in base_models.items():
    fitted_original[name] = evaluate(name, m, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, results_original)

df_results_original = pd.DataFrame(results_original).T.sort_values('Recall (churn)', ascending=False)

Observation: on the raw imbalanced data, boosting methods (XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting) already lead on ROC-AUC, consistent with boosting's sequential error-correction handling the minority class better than bagging without any resampling. Single Decision Tree lags on precision/ROC-AUC as expected from a high-variance single model. This is the baseline against which SMOTE/undersampling are compared next.

5. Model Building — SMOTE-Oversampled Data¶

SMOTE synthesizes new minority-class (churn) samples in feature space so the training set is balanced 50/50 — applied to the training set only, after the split, so the test set remains a realistic, untouched sample of the real-world class distribution.

In [22]:
smote = SMOTE(random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
X_train_sm, y_train_sm = smote.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)
print("Before SMOTE:", y_train.value_counts().to_dict())
print("After SMOTE :", y_train_sm.value_counts().to_dict())

results_smote = {}
fitted_smote = {}
for name, m in base_models.items():
    m_fresh = type(m)(**m.get_params())
    fitted_smote[name] = evaluate(name, m_fresh, X_train_sm, y_train_sm, X_test, y_test, results_smote)

df_results_smote = pd.DataFrame(results_smote).T.sort_values('Recall (churn)', ascending=False)
df_results_smote.round(3)

6. Model Building — Undersampled Data¶

Random undersampling drops majority-class (existing-customer) rows to match the minority class count — training set shrinks substantially, trading data volume for balance.

6.1 Comparing the three resampling strategies¶

In [24]:
comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    'Original (best F1)': df_results_original['F1 (churn)'],
    'SMOTE (best F1)': df_results_smote['F1 (churn)'],
    'Undersampled (best F1)': df_results_under['F1 (churn)'],
}).round(3)
comparison['Original Recall'] = df_results_original['Recall (churn)'].round(3)
comparison['SMOTE Recall'] = df_results_smote['Recall (churn)'].round(3)
comparison['Undersampled Recall'] = df_results_under['Recall (churn)'].round(3)
comparison[['Original Recall','SMOTE Recall','Undersampled Recall','Original (best F1)','SMOTE (best F1)','Undersampled (best F1)']]
Out[24]:
Original Recall SMOTE Recall Undersampled Recall Original (best F1) SMOTE (best F1) Undersampled (best F1)
AdaBoost 0.729 0.837 0.917 0.807 0.779 0.748
Bagging 0.812 0.855 0.902 0.848 0.857 0.818
Decision Tree 0.803 0.825 0.889 0.802 0.794 0.747
Gradient Boosting 0.806 0.871 0.923 0.875 0.872 0.847
LightGBM 0.865 0.877 0.942 0.902 0.889 0.857
Random Forest 0.772 0.840 0.920 0.841 0.848 0.807
XGBoost 0.865 0.874 0.942 0.899 0.892 0.864

Decision — carrying SMOTE forward:

  • Undersampling raises recall somewhat but at a real cost: the training set drops to ~2,600 rows (from ~8,100), discarding a large majority of legitimate "existing customer" examples the model could have learned from — this shows up as lower precision/F1 for most models above, i.e. more false alarms.
  • SMOTE raises churn recall over the original imbalanced data for nearly every model without shrinking the dataset, since it synthesizes additional minority examples rather than deleting majority ones.
  • Original (no resampling) already performs competitively for the boosting models specifically, since boosting's loss reweighting partially compensates for imbalance on its own — but recall is still lower than with SMOTE across the board.

SMOTE is carried forward for hyperparameter tuning and the final model: it improves minority-class recall (the metric that matters most for catching churners before they leave) while preserving the full training set size, and it's the more defensible choice for a bank that would rather review a few extra false-positive retention offers than silently miss real churners.

7. Hyperparameter Tuning¶

Tuning the three strongest models from the SMOTE comparison above: LightGBM, XGBoost, and Random Forest — chosen because they led on recall/F1 in section 6 and represent two different ensembling strategies (boosting vs. bagging), giving the tuning step real coverage rather than tuning three near-identical boosters. RandomizedSearchCV is used over GridSearchCV for the boosters given their larger parameter spaces, to keep search time reasonable while still covering the space well (compute here is intentionally kept modest — a single-core environment — so n_iter/cv are set for a fast, still-representative search; widen them if running with more cores available).

In [25]:
from scipy.stats import randint, uniform

param_dist = {
    'LightGBM': {
        'n_estimators': randint(100, 300),
        'num_leaves': randint(15, 63),
        'learning_rate': uniform(0.03, 0.17),
        'max_depth': randint(3, 10),
    },
    'XGBoost': {
        'n_estimators': randint(100, 300),
        'max_depth': randint(3, 8),
        'learning_rate': uniform(0.03, 0.17),
        'subsample': uniform(0.7, 0.3),
    },
    'Random Forest': {
        'n_estimators': randint(100, 250),
        'max_depth': randint(5, 20),
        'min_samples_split': randint(2, 10),
    },
}

tune_models = {
    'LightGBM': LGBMClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, verbose=-1, n_jobs=1),
    'XGBoost': XGBClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, eval_metric='logloss', n_jobs=1),
    'Random Forest': RandomForestClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=1),
}

best_models = {}
for name, model in tune_models.items():
    print(f"Tuning {name}...")
    search = RandomizedSearchCV(
        model, param_dist[name], n_iter=6, cv=3, scoring='recall',
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=1
    )
    search.fit(X_train_sm, y_train_sm)
    best_models[name] = search.best_estimator_
    print(f"  Best params: {search.best_params_}")
    print(f"  Best CV recall: {search.best_score_:.3f}\n")

8. Stacked Ensemble¶

Combining the three tuned models as base learners with a logistic regression meta-learner, which learns how to weight each base model's predictions rather than averaging them naively.

In [27]:
stacked_model = StackingClassifier(
    estimators=[(name.replace(' ', '_'), model) for name, model in best_models.items()],
    final_estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    cv=3, n_jobs=1
)
stacked_model.fit(X_train_sm, y_train_sm)

pred = stacked_model.predict(X_test)
proba = stacked_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
stacked_results = {
    'Recall (churn)': recall_score(y_test, pred),
    'Precision (churn)': precision_score(y_test, pred),
    'F1 (churn)': f1_score(y_test, pred),
    'Accuracy': accuracy_score(y_test, pred),
    'ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_test, proba),
}
print("Stacked Ensemble performance:")
for k, v in stacked_results.items():
    print(f"  {k}: {v:.3f}")

best_models['Stacked Ensemble'] = stacked_model
results_tuned['Stacked Ensemble'] = stacked_results

Selection rationale: the model above is chosen by highest F1 on the churn class — the metric that balances catching churners (recall) against not overwhelming the retention team with false alarms (precision). Looking at the full comparison table: the tuned boosters (LightGBM/XGBoost) and the stacked ensemble are close on F1, with the stacked ensemble typically edging out slightly on recall at a small precision cost. Given a bank retention use case, a small recall gain is usually worth a modest rise in false positives (a wasted retention call is far cheaper than a lost customer — quantified explicitly in the cost analysis below), which is why the comparison and cost analysis are read together rather than the F1 ranking alone deciding the outcome.

Global feature importance via SHAP summary plot, plus individual waterfall plots for a true positive (correctly caught churner), a false negative (missed churner — the costliest error), and a false positive (false alarm), to see why the model made each call.

11. Cost-Sensitive Threshold Analysis¶

Translating the confusion matrix into rupees. Assumptions (stated explicitly, adjustable):

  • Cost of a false negative (missed churner, customer leaves): ≈ ₹20,000 — approximate lost annual fee + interest + interchange revenue from a departing cardholder.
  • Cost of a false positive (unnecessary retention outreach to a customer who wasn't leaving): ≈ ₹500 — cost of a retention call/offer/discount extended to a customer who didn't need it.

These are illustrative planning assumptions, not confirmed bank figures — the analysis below is about how to pick a threshold given cost ratios, and the ₹500/₹20,000 numbers can be swapped for the bank's real figures without changing the method.

In [36]:
COST_FN = 20000  # rupees, cost of missing a churner
COST_FP = 500     # rupees, cost of an unnecessary retention offer

proba_final = final_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
thresholds = np.arange(0.01, 0.96, 0.02)
costs = []

for t in thresholds:
    pred_t = (proba_final >= t).astype(int)
    fn = ((y_test == 1) & (pred_t == 0)).sum()
    fp = ((y_test == 0) & (pred_t == 1)).sum()
    total_cost = fn * COST_FN + fp * COST_FP
    costs.append(total_cost)

costs = np.array(costs)
best_t_idx = costs.argmin()
best_t = thresholds[best_t_idx]

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.plot(thresholds, costs / 1e5, marker='o', markersize=3)
plt.axvline(best_t, color='red', linestyle='--', label=f'Min-cost threshold = {best_t:.2f}')
plt.axvline(0.5, color='gray', linestyle=':', label='Default threshold = 0.50')
plt.xlabel('Classification threshold')
plt.ylabel('Total expected cost (₹ lakh)')
plt.title('Total Cost vs. Classification Threshold')
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

default_pred = (proba_final >= 0.5).astype(int)
default_fn = ((y_test == 1) & (default_pred == 0)).sum()
default_fp = ((y_test == 0) & (default_pred == 1)).sum()
default_cost = default_fn * COST_FN + default_fp * COST_FP

print(f"Default threshold (0.50): FN={default_fn}, FP={default_fp}, total cost = ₹{default_cost:,}")
print(f"Optimal threshold ({best_t:.2f}): FN={costs.argmin()}, total cost = ₹{costs.min():,.0f}")
print(f"Estimated saving on this test set by moving to the cost-optimal threshold: ₹{default_cost - costs.min():,.0f}")
print(f"\nFN count at optimal threshold: {int(((y_test==1) & ((proba_final >= best_t).astype(int)==0)).sum())}")
print(f"FP count at optimal threshold: {int(((y_test==0) & ((proba_final >= best_t).astype(int)==1)).sum())}")

Default threshold (0.50): FN=40, FP=34, total cost = ₹817,000
Optimal threshold (0.01): FN=0, total cost = ₹181,500
Estimated saving on this test set by moving to the cost-optimal threshold: ₹635,500

FN count at optimal threshold: 1
FP count at optimal threshold: 323

Reading this: because a missed churner (₹20,000) is modeled as far more expensive than a false alarm (₹500) — a 40x cost ratio — the cost-minimizing threshold sits well below the default 0.50, low enough that the model catches essentially every churner in the test set (FN≈0) and the remaining cost is almost entirely false alarms. That the optimum sits near the low end of the sweep isn't a search artifact — it's the direct, correct consequence of the assumed cost ratio: when missing a customer is ~40x more expensive than an unnecessary retention call, the model should flag aggressively.

This is also a useful sanity check on the cost assumptions themselves: if a 40x FN:FP ratio pushes the optimal policy to "flag almost everyone above a very low score," that's worth validating against the bank's real operational capacity — a retention team can't act on flags for the whole customer base. In practice this argues for either (a) confirming the FN cost is genuinely that high relative to FP cost, or (b) adding a capacity constraint (e.g., "flag the top N% highest-risk customers per month") on top of the pure cost-minimization threshold, since an unconstrained optimum will keep pushing toward flagging more people as long as FN stays this expensive.

12. Calibration Check¶

The cost analysis above assumes predict_proba() outputs are reasonably trustworthy probabilities, not just a ranking score. Boosted tree models are known to be somewhat overconfident/miscalibrated out of the box — checking that explicitly before relying on the threshold above.

In [37]:
prob_true, prob_pred = calibration_curve(y_test, proba_final, n_bins=10)

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
plt.plot(prob_pred, prob_true, marker='o', label=FINAL_MODEL_NAME)
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', label='Perfectly calibrated')
plt.xlabel('Mean predicted probability')
plt.ylabel('Observed churn rate')
plt.title('Calibration Curve — Final Model')
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Reading this: if the curve tracks the diagonal reasonably closely, the model's probabilities are usable as-is for the cost-threshold analysis above. Meaningful deviation (e.g., predicted 0.7 but observed churn rate is actually 0.5) would mean the raw probabilities overstate confidence, and a calibration step (Platt scaling / isotonic regression via CalibratedClassifierCV) should be applied before trusting the rupee-optimal threshold. Noting this explicitly is the difference between an academically "best" model and one that is safe to actually operate a retention program against.

Insights (what the data and model show)¶

  1. Transaction activity is the dominant churn signal. Total_Trans_Ct and Total_Trans_Amt rank among the top SHAP drivers, consistent with the EDA medians in section 2.4 — attrited customers transact meaningfully less than existing ones well before the account is formally closed.
  2. Revolving balance decline is an early-warning signal. Low Total_Revolving_Bal combined with low utilization tracks with churn — customers appear to wind down usage before leaving rather than leaving abruptly.
  3. Inactivity precedes attrition. Months_Inactive_12_mon is both a strong EDA separator and a top SHAP feature — a concrete, monitorable trigger (e.g., 2+ consecutive inactive months) rather than an abstract risk score.
  4. Relationship depth matters. Total_Relationship_Count (number of products held) shows up as protective — customers with more products/services are stickier, a classic cross-sell retention lever.
  5. The model materially outperforms a naive baseline. The final model selected in section 9 achieves the recall/precision/ROC-AUC reported there versus a ~16% churn base rate — i.e., flagging at-risk customers with a small fraction of false alarms relative to flagging everyone.

Business recommendations (what the bank should do)¶

  1. Build an inactivity trigger. Auto-flag customers after 2 consecutive inactive months for a low-cost re-engagement touch (app notification, cashback nudge) — cheap relative to the ₹20,000 assumed cost of losing the customer entirely.
  2. Operate the model at the cost-optimal threshold, not 0.50. Section 11 shows the optimal threshold is lower than default given the FN/FP cost asymmetry — deploying at 0.50 leaves real money on the table.
  3. Prioritize retention spend by SHAP-driven risk drivers, not a flat offer to everyone flagged: customers whose top SHAP contributors are declining transaction count/amount are good candidates for spend-based incentives (bonus rewards on the next N transactions); customers whose top driver is inactivity are better candidates for a re-engagement nudge than a discount.
  4. Cross-sell to increase Total_Relationship_Count. Since product depth is protective, bundling a second product (savings account, another card tier) for single-product customers is a plausible retention lever worth A/B testing.
  5. Re-run the calibration check periodically. If the model is redeployed on new data, recheck calibration (section 12) before trusting the ₹-based threshold — a model that drifts out of calibration will silently make the cost-optimal threshold wrong.

14. Leakage-Aware Ablation Study¶

Why this matters: Total_Trans_Ct, Total_Trans_Amt, Total_Revolving_Bal, Total_Amt_Chng_Q4_Q1, and Total_Ct_Chng_Q4_Q1 are all aggregated over the trailing 12 months — the same window that overlaps with a customer's actual attrition. For a customer who has already started disengaging (fewer transactions, declining balance) before formally closing the account, these features partly describe the churn in progress rather than an early warning signal from stable account/demographic attributes. This is a known concern with this dataset and a strong ROC-AUC alone (as reported in section 9) does not rule it out — it needs to be measured, not just noted.

Method: retrain the same tuned-LightGBM pipeline (same SMOTE + RandomizedSearchCV setup as section 7) on two feature sets:

  1. Full feature set — everything used in the main analysis (sections 3–9).
  2. Leakage-robust set — the five trailing-activity features above removed, leaving only demographic, tenure, credit-limit, and utilization-style features that don't directly encode the customer's most recent behavioral decline.
In [39]:
LEAKY_FEATURES = [
    'Total_Trans_Ct', 'Total_Trans_Amt', 'Total_Revolving_Bal',
    'Total_Amt_Chng_Q4_Q1', 'Total_Ct_Chng_Q4_Q1'
]

X_train_ablated = X_train.drop(columns=LEAKY_FEATURES)
X_test_ablated = X_test.drop(columns=LEAKY_FEATURES)

smote_ablated = SMOTE(random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
X_train_ablated_sm, y_train_ablated_sm = smote_ablated.fit_resample(X_train_ablated, y_train)

ablated_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    LGBMClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, verbose=-1, n_jobs=1),
    param_dist['LightGBM'], n_iter=6, cv=3, scoring='recall',
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=1
)
ablated_search.fit(X_train_ablated_sm, y_train_ablated_sm)
ablated_model = ablated_search.best_estimator_

pred_ablated = ablated_model.predict(X_test_ablated)
proba_ablated = ablated_model.predict_proba(X_test_ablated)[:, 1]

ablation_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'Full feature set (final model)': {
        'Recall (churn)': recall_score(y_test, final_model.predict(X_test)),
        'Precision (churn)': precision_score(y_test, final_model.predict(X_test)),
        'F1 (churn)': f1_score(y_test, final_model.predict(X_test)),
        'ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_test, final_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]),
    },
    'Leakage-robust set (activity features removed)': {
        'Recall (churn)': recall_score(y_test, pred_ablated),
        'Precision (churn)': precision_score(y_test, pred_ablated),
        'F1 (churn)': f1_score(y_test, pred_ablated),
        'ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_test, proba_ablated),
    },
}).round(4)
ablation_summary

Reading this result: removing the trailing-12-month activity features drops ROC-AUC from ~0.99 to ~0.84 and, more importantly, recall on the churn class falls from ~88% to ~43% — the model goes from catching roughly 9 in 10 churners to catching fewer than half. This is a substantial, not marginal, drop.

What this means for how the headline model should be read:

  • The full-feature model (used throughout sections 4–13) is genuinely strong at identifying customers who are already in the process of disengaging — which is still operationally useful (it's a real, actionable "this account is winding down right now" signal for the retention team) — but it should not be sold as a long-horizon early-warning system, since most of its lift comes from features that move in the weeks/months immediately around attrition.
  • The leakage-robust model (ROC-AUC 0.84, recall 43%) is a more honest estimate of how well purely structural signals (tenure, credit limit, relationship depth, demographics) predict churn on their own, absent recent behavioral decline. An AUC of 0.84 is still meaningfully better than random and a legitimate result to report — it's just a different, harder question than the headline number answers.
  • What would resolve this properly: this dataset has no transaction-level timestamps, so a true out-of-time validation (train on behavior through month T, predict attrition after T+k) isn't possible here. If Thera Bank's real data includes timestamps, the correct fix is a temporal train/test split with a defined prediction lead time (e.g., "predict churn in the next 90 days using only data through today"), which this ablation approximates but cannot fully replace.

This caveat is carried into the Limitations section below and should be stated up front in any write-up of this project's headline ROC-AUC.

15. K-Fold Cross-Validation — Stability Check on the Final Comparison¶

Section 9's model comparison used a single 80/20 train/test split. A single split can make a model look better (or worse) than it typically performs purely by chance in how the split happened to fall. To check that, the final model and its top competitors are re-evaluated with 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set, using the same tuned hyperparameters found in section 7.

Leakage-safe setup: SMOTE is applied inside each CV fold via an imblearn pipeline (fit on that fold's training portion only) rather than once on the whole training set beforehand — otherwise synthetic points derived from a validation fold's neighbors could leak into that same fold's evaluation.

In [41]:
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline

# Rebuild each tuned model with its already-found best hyperparameters (from section 7),
# so cross-validation measures the STABILITY of the chosen configuration, not a fresh search per fold.
lgbm_params = best_models['LightGBM'].get_params()
xgb_params = best_models['XGBoost'].get_params()
rf_params = best_models['Random Forest'].get_params()

lgbm_cv_model = LGBMClassifier(**lgbm_params)
xgb_cv_model = XGBClassifier(**xgb_params)
rf_cv_model = RandomForestClassifier(**rf_params)

stacked_cv_model = StackingClassifier(
    estimators=[('LightGBM', LGBMClassifier(**lgbm_params)),
                ('XGBoost', XGBClassifier(**xgb_params)),
                ('Random_Forest', RandomForestClassifier(**rf_params))],
    final_estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    cv=3, n_jobs=1
)

cv_models = {
    'LightGBM (final model)': lgbm_cv_model,
    'XGBoost': xgb_cv_model,
    'Random Forest': rf_cv_model,
    'Stacked Ensemble': stacked_cv_model,
}

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
scoring = ['recall', 'precision', 'f1', 'roc_auc']

cv_results = {}
for name, model in cv_models.items():
    pipe = ImbPipeline([('smote', SMOTE(random_state=RANDOM_STATE)), ('clf', model)])
    cv_res = cross_validate(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=skf, scoring=scoring, n_jobs=1)
    cv_results[name] = {
        'Recall mean': cv_res['test_recall'].mean(), 'Recall std': cv_res['test_recall'].std(),
        'Precision mean': cv_res['test_precision'].mean(), 'Precision std': cv_res['test_precision'].std(),
        'F1 mean': cv_res['test_f1'].mean(), 'F1 std': cv_res['test_f1'].std(),
        'ROC-AUC mean': cv_res['test_roc_auc'].mean(), 'ROC-AUC std': cv_res['test_roc_auc'].std(),
    }

df_cv_summary = pd.DataFrame(cv_results).T.round(4)
df_cv_summary

Reading this: the standard deviations across folds are small (roughly 0.01–0.02 on recall/F1, ~0.001–0.002 on ROC-AUC) for every model, meaning the section 9 single-split ranking wasn't a fluke of that particular split — the relative ordering (LightGBM/Stacked Ensemble ahead of XGBoost, all three ahead of Random Forest) holds up under resampling. The CV means are also slightly higher than the single-split test numbers in section 9 for every model, which is expected: the single test-split numbers include some fold-specific variance the CV mean averages out.

LightGBM and the Stacked Ensemble are statistically indistinguishable on this evidence — their means differ by less than one standard deviation on every metric. Given that, the choice to ship LightGBM alone over the stacked ensemble is a complexity/maintainability call, not a performance one: a single LightGBM model is simpler to serve, monitor, and explain to a regulator or business stakeholder than a 3-model stack with a logistic meta-learner, for statistically the same result — which is a legitimate and defensible reason to prefer it in a production setting.

16. Limitations & What I'd Do With More Time¶

Honest constraints on this analysis, stated explicitly rather than left for a reviewer to discover:

1. Temporal leakage risk (measured, not just suspected). As shown in section 14, removing the trailing-12-month activity features (Total_Trans_Ct, Total_Trans_Amt, Total_Revolving_Bal, Total_Amt_Chng_Q4_Q1, Total_Ct_Chng_Q4_Q1) drops ROC-AUC from 0.990 to 0.837 and churn recall from 88% to 43%. Most of this model's predictive power comes from features that describe a customer's behavior as they are already disengaging, not from stable, early-warning signal. The headline 0.99 ROC-AUC should be read as "this model reliably identifies customers who are already winding down their account," not "this model predicts churn months in advance." Both are useful to a bank, but they are different products with different deployment implications.

2. No true out-of-time validation. This dataset has no transaction-level timestamps, so a proper temporal train/test split (train on data through month T, evaluate on attrition after T+k) isn't possible here. The ablation in section 14 is the closest available proxy. If Thera Bank's internal data includes timestamps, that split should replace this analysis before any production deployment decision.

3. Cost assumptions are illustrative, not confirmed. The ₹20,000 (false negative) / ₹500 (false positive) figures used in section 11 are reasonable planning assumptions, not validated bank figures. The method (sweep thresholds, minimize expected cost) is sound and reusable — swapping in Thera Bank's real customer lifetime value and retention-outreach cost would change the optimal threshold without changing the approach.

4. The cost-optimal threshold implies flagging most at-risk-looking customers, which needs a capacity constraint in practice. Section 11 found the unconstrained cost-optimal threshold sits very low (near-zero false negatives), which is correct given the assumed 40x cost ratio, but a retention team has finite capacity. A real deployment should combine this with a "flag the top N% by predicted risk" cap, not an unconstrained cost minimum.

5. Small-sample caution on Card_Category. The dataset is overwhelmingly Blue-tier cardholders (see section 2.3); churn-rate differences and SHAP attributions involving Gold/Platinum/Silver dummy variables are based on a much smaller sample and should be treated as directional, not precise.

6. Single dataset snapshot. All evaluation (including the 5-fold CV in section 15) is internal cross-validation on one historical extract. It confirms the model is stable on this data, not that it will generalize to future customer cohorts or a shifted product mix — ongoing monitoring for feature/prediction drift would be needed in production (see the /predict API note on this below).

What I'd do with more time:

  • Get timestamped transaction data and run a genuine temporal validation instead of the section 14 proxy.
  • Validate the ₹ cost assumptions against Thera Bank's actual finance data.
  • Add a capacity-constrained decision layer on top of the cost-optimal threshold.
  • Build a drift-monitoring check comparing incoming prediction-time feature distributions against the training distribution, to catch the model silently going stale.
